title: What worked, what failed, and what remains open
audience: Public mathematical exploration; no prior conversation assumed
meaning: A retrospective on explicitly tested rules, not a claim that every possible zeta-based approach is impossible.

scenes.title: A four-color brush is a display rule
scenes.narration: This idea starts with a four-color quadrant brush at each point. Its trail changes with direction, overlap, rotation, and resolution. That makes the geometry visible. But a surviving pixel color is not, by itself, an arithmetic certificate of primality.
screenLines: An arithmetic claim needs a separate test

scenes.title: A downward slope did not identify primes
scenes.narration: Z three means the third zeta zero, not twenty-three or a prime label. For the first hundred zero indices, negative starting slopes occurred at fourteen prime indices and thirty-five composite indices. Eleven prime indices sloped upward. Both signs mix the classes, so this proposed rule fails.
screenLines: Initial paths: ζ(s)=a, starting at a=0
scenes.cohortNote: Index 1 is neither prime nor composite and has a negative initial slope.
scenes.status: COUNTEREXAMPLES TO THE PROPOSED SLOPE RULE

scenes.title: Substituting the half-unit expression
scenes.narration: The proposed denominator, g of n, simplifies exactly to n. Substituting it into zeta's series leaves the same function where that series converges. The half inside g does not set s to one half. And ninety-seven and composite ninety-nine both have a fractional half when divided by two.
screenLines: The half inside g(n) does not set s = 1/2
scenes.status: EXACT SUBSTITUTION • THE ZETA SERIES IS UNCHANGED

scenes.title: One half is a line coordinate
scenes.narration: Zeta at one half exists and is about minus one point four six. The critical line instead uses one half plus i t. Particular heights give zeros. Putting ninety-seven into t gives a nonzero complex value. Fixing the real part does not identify an integer as prime.
screenLines: RH conjecture: all nontrivial zeros lie on this line
scenes.status: A ZETA ZERO IS NOT AN INDIVIDUAL PRIME LABEL

scenes.title: Extra zeta colors did not fix the test
scenes.narration: With integer n used as height, ninety-seven and composite ninety-nine both occupy quadrant one. Comparing zeta at s, s plus one, and s minus one still fails. Matching ninety-seven's three colors keeps six primes and eighteen composites, while missing nineteen primes between two and one hundred.
screenLines: 97 and 99 share the original quadrant I

scenes.title: Switching the unit term changes the target
scenes.narration: Removing the unit term gives zeta minus one. Its zeros are where zeta equals one. Multiplying the two functions combines both zero sets. Every hypothetical off-line zeta zero survives, so the switch does not prove the hypothesis.
screenLines: 1 is a unit; it is not prime

scenes.title: Reversal does not create the complement
scenes.narration: Reordering the same finite sum leaves its value unchanged. For the tested coefficient reversal, subtracting the reverse makes opposite positions have opposite signs. A nonzero, nonnegative composite indicator cannot have that symmetry. Other definitions of a backward recurrence would need a separate derivation.
screenLines: Through 10: prime polynomial difference = z² − z⁸
scenes.status: THE TESTED REVERSAL DOES NOT ISOLATE COMPOSITES

scenes.title: Finite cancellation is well defined
scenes.narration: Finite subtraction leaves nonprimes but requires knowing the prime terms to remove. At s equals minus one, the ordinary integer series diverges. Zeta's continued value, minus one twelfth, is not an ordinary sum for subtracting infinitely many primes.
screenLines: 1 remains nonprime, but is not composite

scenes.title: Prime terms really can cancel
scenes.narration: For real s greater than one, define A as the odd-number part of zeta. Then A minus one minus log A cancels every odd-prime coefficient and leaves weighted odd composites. The coefficient at ninety-seven is zero; at ninety-nine it is one. Evaluating H at ninety-seven does not extract that coefficient.
scenes.status: EXACT COEFFICIENT IDENTITY • NO SPEEDUP ESTABLISHED

scenes.title: A correct color test still does arithmetic
scenes.narration: Wilson's theorem tests a candidate without a list of previous primes. Our encoding places primes in quadrant one. The modular factorial supplies the answer; color displays it. This is not instantaneous. The separate four-divisor color test works only within its stated range.
screenLines: R(n) = 0 exactly when n is prime
Four fixed divisors suffice through 100, not for all n
scenes.status: CORRECT CLASSICAL TEST • NO NEW FAST ALGORITHM

scenes.title: What the finite experiment establishes
scenes.narration: Removing trivial factor pairs leaves an exact composite remainder. For odd integers greater than one, D counts nontrivial pairs: zero for ninety-seven, two for ninety-nine. The proof covers that entire domain. The implementation was independently checked through one hundred thousand. It still performs divisor counting.
screenLines: D(n) counts pairs n = ab with 3 ≤ a ≤ b
For odd n > 1: D(n)=0 exactly when n is prime
scenes.status: PROVED CLASSICAL IDENTITY + FINITE IMPLEMENTATION CHECKS

scenes.title: Useful next steps have explicit checks
scenes.narration: The contribution is reproducible tests and counterexamples. Phase plots can guide searches; rigorous bounds must certify the zero count. Prime extraction also needs error bounds and cost comparisons. These experiments establish no new prime algorithm or Riemann Hypothesis advance.
screenLines: Visual candidate → certified contour → zero count
Coefficient extraction → error bound → cost comparison
Finite examples do not settle the infinite problem
Reusable evidence, not an RH proof
